::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
lizards <- read_csv("data/lizards-spring-2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_missing_morph <- sum(lizards$exclusion == "missing morphology", na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::


The model estimates both links of the paradigm jointly, morphology →
performance and performance → survival, while correcting survival for
imperfect detection. The choices behind the data inputs are explained on
the [Data page](01-data.qmd). A [PDF version](02-model.pdf) of this
page is also available.

## Causal diagram

![Causal structure of the model. Solid arrows are present in both models. The dashed arrow (direct effects $\gamma$) is present only in M2. Sex affects performance ($\delta$), survival ($c$) and detection ($\zeta$). Body temperature at the trial affects sprint and bite ($t$).](figures/causal-diagram.svg){width=100%}

## Transformations

All continuous variables except body temperature are log-transformed.
All, including temperature, are then standardised within species,
using that species' observed sample mean and SD:
$$
\operatorname{std}_s(v) = \frac{v - \bar{v}_s}{\operatorname{sd}_s(v)}.
$$
Coefficients are then in within-species SD units, and so comparable
among species and traits. Survival coefficients become standardised
selection gradients (on the logit scale), and one set of generic
priors can be used. The constants $\bar v_s$ and $\operatorname{sd}_s(v)$
are fixed data, so the simulator used for calibration applies the identical
transformation (`prepare_data()` in `R/prepare-data.R`).

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $i = 1, \dots, N$ | individual |
| $s = s[i] \in \{\text{caro}, \text{cris}, \text{sag}\}$ | species of individual $i$ |
| $j \in \{\text{spr}, \text{bite}, \text{bark}, \text{leaf}\}$ | performance trait |
| $k \in \{\text{svl}, \text{hl}, \text{hw}, \text{toe}, \text{pad}\}$ | morphological predictor |
| $k(j)$ | shape trait linked to $j$: $k(\text{spr}) = \text{hl}$, $k(\text{bite}) = \text{hw}$, $k(\text{bark}) = \text{toe}$, $k(\text{leaf}) = \text{pad}$ |
| $m_i \in \{0, 1\}$ | male indicator (female = 0) |
| $x_{ik}$ | standardised morphological predictor (data) |
| $w_{ij}$ | standardised body temperature at the trial for $j$ (data; 0 for bark and leaf) |
| $u_{ij}$ | standardised log performance (data, or latent if missing) |
| $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ | alive at the fall 2024 census (latent) |
| $y_{i2}, y_{i3} \in \{0, 1\}$ | seen in fall 2024 / spring 2025 |

## Performance submodel

Each lizard's vector of the four performance traits is multivariate
normal:
$$
\mathbf{u}_i \sim \operatorname{MVN}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{s[i]}\right),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s = \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_s)\, \boldsymbol{\Omega}\, \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_s),
$$
with a mean that depends on size, the linked shape trait, sex and body
temperature:
$$
\mu_{ij} = \alpha_{sj} + \delta_{sj}\, m_i + b^{\text{svl}}_{sj}\, x_{i,\text{svl}} + b^{\text{shape}}_{sj}\, x_{i,k(j)} + t_{sj}\, w_{ij}.
$$

- $\alpha_{sj}$ is the expected performance of a female of average size
  and shape, tested at the species' mean temperature.
- $t_{sj}$ is the effect of body temperature during the trial. It is
  estimated for sprint and bite only, and fixed at 0 for both
  clinging traits.
  Temperature is a condition of the trial, not a trait of the lizard.
  Survival therefore depends on temperature-adjusted performance,
  $\tilde u_{ij} = u_{ij} - t_{sj}\, w_{ij}$: the lizard's expected
  performance at its species' mean test temperature.
- $\delta_{sj}$ is the male--female difference in performance not
  explained by morphology.
- $b^{\text{svl}}_{sj}$ and $b^{\text{shape}}_{sj}$ are the size and
  shape effects on performance (the first link of the paradigm).
- $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ is a residual correlation matrix shared across
  species. It captures lizards that perform well on all tasks for
  reasons beyond the measured morphology, such as condition or
  motivation.
- Missing $u_{ij}$ are parameters drawn from the same distribution, so
  lizards with missing performance still contribute their survival
  information. This assumes values are missing at random given
  morphology, sex and the other performance traits.
- Leaf-clinging zeros are left-censored. For those lizards,
  $u_{i,\text{leaf}}$ is also a parameter, but it is constrained to lie
  below the detection limit,
  $$
  u_{i,\text{leaf}} < c_s = \operatorname{std}_s(\log 0.01),
  $$
  and follows the same multivariate normal distribution. They therefore
  count as the weakest leaf clingers, rather than being dropped or given
  an arbitrary value. The standardisation constants for leaf clinging
  are computed from the non-zero values.

## Survival and detection submodel

The probability of surviving the first six months depends on
temperature-adjusted performance:
$$
z_i \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\phi_i),
$$
$$
\operatorname{logit}(\phi_i) = a_s + c_s\, m_i + \sum_j \beta_{sj}\, \tilde u_{ij} + \sum_j q_{sj}\, \tilde u_{ij}^2 \;\left[\, + \sum_k \gamma_{sk}\, x_{ik} \,\right]_{\text{M2 only}}.
$$

- $a_s$ is the logit 6-month survival of an average female.
- $c_s$ is the sex difference in survival.
- $\beta_{sj}$ is linear selection on performance $j$, and $q_{sj}$ is
  quadratic selection. $q < 0$ is stabilising and $q > 0$ disruptive.
  The conventional quadratic gradient is $2q_{sj}$.
- $\gamma_{sk}$ is the direct effect of morphology on survival. It is
  fixed at 0 in M1. Including $x_{i,\text{svl}}$ here guards against
  attributing size-related survival to performance.
- Correlational selection ($\tilde u_{ij} \tilde u_{ij'}$ terms) is not included.

Resighting depends on whether the lizard is alive:
$$
y_{i2} \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(z_i\, p_i), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(p_i) = \pi_s + \zeta_p\, m_i,
$$
$$
y_{i3} \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(z_i\, \lambda_i), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(\lambda_i) = \ell_s + \zeta_\lambda\, m_i.
$$

- $p_i$ is the probability of detection in fall given the lizard is
  alive.
- $\lambda_i$ is the probability of being seen in spring 2025 given the
  lizard was alive in fall. It combines fall-to-spring survival and
  spring detection, which three occasions cannot separate. It is a
  nuisance parameter.
- The sex effects on detection, $\zeta_p$ and $\zeta_\lambda$, are shared
  across species. Males display and may be more conspicuous.

This is a Cormack--Jolly--Seber model for three occasions. Summing over
the latent $z_i$ gives the likelihood of each history:

| History $(y_{i2}, y_{i3})$ | Probability |
|---|---|
| 1 1 | $\phi_i\, p_i\, \lambda_i$ |
| 0 1 | $\phi_i\, (1 - p_i)\, \lambda_i$ |
| 1 0 | $\phi_i\, p_i\, (1 - \lambda_i)$ |
| 0 0 | $(1 - \phi_i) + \phi_i\, (1 - p_i)(1 - \lambda_i)$ |

Lizards seen in spring 2025 but missed in fall (history 01) identify
$p$. Selection on 6-month survival ($\phi$) is then estimated free of
detection bias. This assumes detection does not depend on performance
or morphology beyond sex.

## Derived quantities

For morphological predictor $k$ in species $s$, evaluated at the
species mean, where $\tilde u = 0$ so the quadratic terms vanish:
$$
\text{indirect}_{sk} = \sum_{j} b_{sjk}\, \beta_{sj},
\qquad
\text{direct}_{sk} = \gamma_{sk},
\qquad
\text{total}_{sk} = \text{indirect}_{sk} + \text{direct}_{sk}.
$$
Here $b_{sjk}$ is $b^{\text{svl}}_{sj}$ for $k = \text{svl}$,
$b^{\text{shape}}_{sj}$ when $k = k(j)$, and 0 otherwise. Size is the
only predictor with indirect paths through all four performance traits.
Support for full mediation is assessed in three ways: from the
posteriors of $\gamma_{sk}$, by comparing M1 and M2 with PSIS-LOO, and
by checking in simulation ([Validation](03-validation.qmd)) whether the design can detect
$\gamma \neq 0$.

## Priors

### Hierarchical structure

Every parameter labelled hierarchical below varies by species and is
partially pooled:
$$
\theta_s = \mu_\theta + \tau_\theta\, \tilde\theta_s, \qquad \tilde\theta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
$$
with separate $\mu_\theta$ and $\tau_\theta$ for each performance trait
$j$ or predictor $k$. This is the non-centered form used in Stan. With
only three species, $\tau_\theta$ is weakly identified, so its priors
are deliberately informative.

### Prior distributions

All scales are standardised traits or logits. $\mathcal{N}^+$ is the
half-normal distribution.

| Parameter | Pooling | Prior |
|---|---|---|
| **Performance** | | |
| $\alpha_{sj}$ | none | $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$ |
| $\delta_{sj}$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.5)$ |
| $b^{\text{svl}}_{sj}$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.25)$ |
| $b^{\text{shape}}_{sj}$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.25)$ |
| $t_{sj}$ (sprint, bite) | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.25)$ |
| $\sigma_{sj}$ | none | $\mathcal{N}^+(0, 1)$ |
| $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ | shared | $\operatorname{LKJ}(2)$ |
| **Survival** | | |
| $a_s$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(-1, 1)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.5)$ |
| $c_s$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.5)$ |
| $\beta_{sj}$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.25)$ |
| $q_{sj}$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.25)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.1)$ |
| $\gamma_{sk}$ (M2) | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 0.25)$ |
| **Detection** | | |
| $\pi_s$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1.5)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 1)$ |
| $\ell_s$ | hierarchical | $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1.5)$, $\tau \sim \mathcal{N}^+(0, 1)$ |
| $\zeta_p$, $\zeta_\lambda$ | shared | $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ |

The reasoning behind these priors:

- **Performance intercepts $\alpha_{sj}$** are near 0 by construction,
  because traits are centred within species. They are offset only by
  the sex term, so pooling them adds nothing. A first version used
  $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, but prior predictive simulation showed it allowed
  implausible shifts in performance, for example leaf censoring rates
  above 30% when about 3% is observed. It was tightened to
  $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$.
- **Performance slopes** of $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$ put 95% of the mass
  below about 1 SD of performance per SD of morphology.
- **Residual SDs** $\sigma_{sj}$ must lie below 1, because performance
  is standardised.
- **Baseline survival** $\mu_a \sim \mathcal{N}(-1, 1)$ centres 6-month
  survival near 27%. That is a little above the naive 20%, as expected
  once detection is accounted for.
- **Selection gradients** of $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$ allow odds of
  survival to change up to about 2.7-fold per SD of performance (2 prior
  SDs). The quadratic terms are tighter.
- **Detection intercepts** of $\mathcal{N}(0, 1.5)$ are close to uniform
  on the probability scale.

Prior predictive checks of these priors are on the
[Validation page](03-validation.qmd).

## Assumptions and limitations

- **Performance and morphology are measured without error.** Sprint
  timing resolution violates this mildly.
- **Missing data.** Performance is missing at random given the model.
  The 17 lizards with missing toepad area or hind toe
  length are excluded. Only one of them survived to 6 months.
- **Detection** depends on species and sex only. Movement off the study
  area is indistinguishable from death, so $\phi$ is *apparent*
  survival.
- **Shared residual correlation.** The correlation among performance
  traits, $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$, is the same for all species.
- **Temperature.** Its effect on performance is linear, and it is
  unmeasured for both clinging trials.
- **Claw size.** Relative hind toe length is a stand-in for claw size.
- **No correlational selection.** It could be added as an extension.
- **Three species.** Among-species variances are estimated mostly from
  their priors.
